Case Information: A woman in her early 70s presented with a solitary, asymptomatic lump on her scalp. The lesion was present since birth but showed some growth following minor local trauma a couple of months prior to evaluation. No local inflammation, purulent discharge, or systemic symptoms were reported. Medical history included a benign breast nodule resection in teenage years. Family history notable for father who died of metastatic cutaneous melanoma at 83 years old.
Physical Examination: Physical findings revealed an ill-defined, infiltrated plaque with a normochromic, exophytic nodule on the scalp vertex measuring 4.2 × 3.8 cm. The lesion had a waxy surface with irregular transverse furrows and overlying alopecia. Dermoscopic evaluation showed a homogeneous yellow hue with no visible vascular or pigmented structures and absence of follicular ostia. The lesion was firm and mildly tender to touch, seemed adherent to the underlying bone. No palpable lymph nodes were detected.
Diagnostic Tests: - Imaging Studies:    Brain MRI Title: Paramedian sagittal gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted brain MRI    Description: Demonstrated a nonenhancing tumor with sharp margins in the subcutaneous tissue of the scalp with no underlying bone or intracranial involvement  - Histopathology:    Punch biopsy findings:    - Infiltration by monomorphic cells with ovoid nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm amid fibrous stroma in lower dermis    - Cells without discernible cell membranes, forming whorls and strands around collagen bundles    - No adnexal structures overlying the lesion, epidermis spared      - Immunohistochemistry:    - Strongly positive: vimentin and epithelial membrane antigen (EMA)    - Focally positive: progesterone receptor    - Ki-67: estimated 1% positivity    - Negative: cytokeratins AE1/AE3, S100, CD45, CD68, factor XIII, actin, glial fibrillary acidic protein, and octamer-binding transcription factor 4

Case Information: A previously healthy man in his 30s presented with spontaneous bruising, epistaxis, and haematuria. After starting treatment, the patient developed pyrexia after 12 days. Two days later, he developed tender black spots on the scrotum that progressed to painful ulcers over 8 days. As scrotal ulceration progressed, they enlarged and became necrotic with a black eschar. The development and progression of scrotal ulceration coincided with recovery in neutrophil count from 0.3 × 109/L to 1.2 × 109/L and persistent pyrexia.
Physical Examination: Tender black spots on the scrotum were observed, which progressed to painful ulcers. The ulcers enlarged and became necrotic with a black eschar.
Diagnostic Tests: - Laboratory Tests: Peripheral blood cultures and skin swabs from the lesions did not identify bacterial or viral infection. Neutrophil count increased from 0.3 × 109/L to 1.2 × 109/L.- Imaging Studies: Scrotal ultrasonography showed a subcutaneous hypervascular lesion with no abscess.- Pathology: Histopathology on a skin biopsy showed intense inflammation, necrosis, and mature neutrophils with no evidence of leukemic infiltration. Tissue culture findings for bacteria and mycobacteria were negative.Image Title: Clinical photograph of scrotum and penisImage Description: Shows ulceration and necrosis of penile and scrotal skin with surrounding inflammation.Image Title: Scrotal biopsy histopathologic specimenImage Description: Hematoxylin-eosin stained specimen (original magnification ×20) showing intense inflammation, necrosis, and mature neutrophils.
Final Diagnosis: Scrotal ulceration secondary to induction chemotherapy with ATRA

Options.B: Scrotal ulceration secondary to induction chemotherapy with ATRA

Case Information: A female patient in her early 50s presented with multiple (approximately 10) bluish, partially keratotic papules and nodules on the lower legs. The lesions had been growing very slowly in number and size since age 24 and had been bleeding occasionally after trauma. The patient used a wheelchair due to right-sided hemiparesis and hemianopsia caused by an intracranial hemorrhage. At age 4, she had recurrent seizures. She had lipolymphedema of the lower legs attributed to functional venous insufficiency with insufficient venous pump activity, and had been wearing compression stockings for years. Family history revealed similar conditions in the patient's father and aunt, with the father having died of an intracranial hemorrhage in his early 70s.
Physical Examination: Multiple bluish, partially keratotic papules and nodules on the lower legs. Lipolymphedema of the lower legs was present. Right-sided hemiparesis and hemianopsia were noted.
Diagnostic Tests:
- Sonography: Demonstrated intradermal slow-flow vascular malformations with a maximum diameter of 1.2 cm.

- Histopathology:
  Image Description: Biopsy revealed a well-circumscribed lesion with hyperkeratosis and acanthosis of the epidermis overlying a conglomerate of dilated venous-like malformations with continuous smooth muscle in the upper dermis, partly showing thrombosis.

- Genetic Testing:
  Result: Detection of a heterozygous pathogenic KRIT1 variant.

Case Information: A female patient in her late 20s presented with a 2-year history of multiple, slowly growing, infiltrated erythematous-violaceous patches and plaques, with occasional slight pain extending from her left upper arm to the left side of her chest. No triggers such as local infection, insect bite, or trauma occurred before lesion appearance. She denied fever, weight loss, or fatigue.
Physical Examination: Multiple firm, nonscaly, purple erythematous patches and plaques with irregular borders on her left axilla, medial upper arm, and lateral thoracic region. No extracutaneous involvement was observed.
Diagnostic Tests: - Histopathological examination:    - Thin-walled, irregularly branched blood vessels dispersed between thickened collagen bundles    - Endothelial cells were plump but displayed no significant cytologic atypia      - Immunohistochemistry results:    - Positive for: CD31, CD34, Ki-67 (<1%)    - Negative for: podoplanin (D2-40), human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)      - Images:    Image A Title: Clinical presentation    Image A Description: Multiple nonscaly, erythematous-violaceous patches and plaques with irregular borders on the patient's left axilla, medial upper arm, and lateral thoracic region        Image B Title: Histopathological examination (hematoxylin-eosin)    Image B Description: Irregularly branched, thin-walled blood vessels dissecting through collagen bundles within the superficial to mid dermis        Image C Title: Detailed histopathology (hematoxylin-eosin)    Image C Description: Irregularly branched, thin-walled blood vessels with plump endothelial cells dispersed between thickened collagen bundles without signs of atypia        Image D Title: Immunohistochemistry    Image D Description: Endothelial cells positive for cluster of differentiation (CD) 31

Case Information: A teenage girl presented with several months of sinus pressure and facial swelling, and several weeks of external deviation of her nasal septum. No significant past medical history was mentioned.

Case Information: A 12-year-old female presented with asymptomatic vulvar edema of 1 month's duration that was previously treated with topical antifungals and corticosteroids with no improvement. She did not report recent travel or sexual relationships. Medical history included growth delay, several months of constipation treated with laxatives, and hemorrhoids.
Physical Examination: Examination revealed swelling, erythema, and palpable induration on the labia minora and majora of the vulva. No lymphadenopathy was palpated in the inguinal region.
Diagnostic Tests: - Laboratory tests: Slight increase in erythrocyte sedimentation rate, normal angiotensin-converting enzyme levels, negative interferon γ release assay. Fecal calprotectin was 297 μg/g (normal <50 μg/g). Negative stool culture and parasite studies.- Imaging studies:  - Chest radiography: Normal  - Intestinal and pelvic MRI: Normal  - Endoscopic study: Revealed ulcers in duodenal bulb, rectum, sigmoid colon, terminal ileum, and cecum. Erythematous and edematous mucosa with aphthous ulcers in sigmoid and rectal region.- Pathology:  - 4mm punch biopsy from right labia majora showed:    Image Description: Intact epidermis with nodular dermatitis composed of non-necrotizing granulomas in superficial and deep dermis  - Additional histological findings: Aggregated nodules of epithelioid histiocytes without necrosis, poorly compact granulomas with ill-defined borders, associated lymphocytic and eosinophilic infiltrate  - Gastric and intestinal endoscopic biopsies: Granulomas in lamina propria not linked to active crypt injury

Case Information: A woman in her 20s presented with a large erythematous indurated plaque involving the face and neck that had been first noted at age 2 years. The plaque progressively increased in size, and similar plaques developed over the back, right dorsal surface of the hand, suprapubic area, and right thigh over the last 4 years. Scarring developed in the plaques over the face and hand during the course of the disease and led to flexion contracture of the hand with limitation of movement. There were no constitutional symptoms. There was no history of trauma preceding these lesions. She had received multiple previous treatments without significant improvement.
Physical Examination: Well-defined erythematous plaque of 7 × 8 cm over the suprapubic area. Additional plaques present on face, neck, back, right dorsal surface of hand, and right thigh. Flexion contracture of the hand with limited movement noted.
Diagnostic Tests:
- Laboratory Tests:
  * Routine hematological and biochemical investigations were normal
  * Mantoux test showed an induration of 2 × 1 mm at 48 hours

- Imaging Studies:
  * Chest radiography was normal

- Pathological Studies:
  * Direct potassium hydroxide preparation: Multiple budding yeast cells and arthrospores observed
  * Skin biopsy: Granulomatous infiltrate with giant cells, lymphocytes, histiocytes, neutrophils, and eosinophils. Hyaline hyphae branching at acute angles with multiple spores and budding yeasts, positive for silver methenamine and periodic acid–Schiff stains
  * Culture: Grew Trichosporon species, identified as Trichosporon mycotoxinivorans through PCR analysis and DNA sequencing

- Images:
  * Figure 1A Title: Erythematous Crusted Plaque Over Suprapubic Area
  * Figure 2A Title: Potassium hydroxide preparation showing fungal elements
  * Figure 2B Title: Periodic acid–Schiff staining showing inflammatory infiltrate and fungal elements
  * Figure 2C Title: Culture plate showing Trichosporon colonies
Final Diagnosis: Primary cutaneous trichosporonosis caused by Trichosporon mycotoxinivorans

Options.B: Deep cutaneous mycosis due to Trichosporon mycotoxinivorans
Options.C: Primary cutaneous trichosporonosis caused by Trichosporon mycotoxinivorans

Case Information: A man in his 20s presented with thickening and swelling of hands after immersion in water, accompanied by burning pruritus for 3 years. The lesions occurred as symmetrical white and transparent papules, white keratosis, excessive wrinkling on the dorsum of hands after water immersion and worsened in summer, and remitted in winter. He was treated with topical tretinoin ointment intermittently at a local clinic with little improvement. The lesions gradually aggravated, and the affected area dispersed to wrists and elbows during past 1.5 years. He attributed these changes to frequent hand washing during the COVID-19 epidemic. No family history of similar skin problems and no history of hyperhidrosis, cystic fibrosis, atopy, or trauma to the hands.
Physical Examination: After immersing both hands in water for 10 mins, there were symmetrical white papules, white hyperkeratosis spots, and excessive wrinkling on the thenar eminence, wrist flexure of both hands, and dorsum of fingers and hands.
Diagnostic Tests: - Skin Biopsy:  Histopathologic examination revealed remarkable compact orthohyperkeratosis in the epidermis, dilatation of intraepidermal eccrine ducts, and hyperplasia of the eccrine sweat glands.  - Images:    Image Title: Clinical presentation after water immersion    Image Description: A and B - Symmetrical white papules, white hyperkeratosis spots, and excessive wrinkling on hands after water immersion        Image Title: Histopathologic features    Image Description: C and D - Hyperkeratosis, dilated eccrine ducts in the epidermis and dermis, and hyperplasia of the eccrine sweat gland (hematoxylin-eosin staining)

Case Information: A woman in her late teens with a 1-year history of viral cardiomyopathy presented with decompensated heart failure. Case Information: A 40-year-old man from eastern India presented with a nonhealing ulcer on the tongue present for the last 4 months. The lesion started as a small painless mass on the right lateral aspect of the tongue, which gradually grew and subsequently ulcerated. It caused mild difficulty in eating. No history of trauma or tongue bite preceding the lesion. Patient denied consuming tobacco or alcohol regularly. Medical history includes well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus for 2 years with oral hypoglycemic agents. No systemic complaints. No history of high-risk behavior for HIV.
Physical Examination: Single well-defined ulcer measuring 2 × 2 cm on the right lateral aspect of tongue with a clean base and irregular and elevated heaped-up margins. No underlying induration, friability, or bleeding on manipulation. Rest of the oral cavity was normal.
Diagnostic Tests: - Histopathological examination (3-mm punch biopsy from edge of ulcer):  - Dense diffuse infiltrate of lymphocytes, histiocytes, epithelioid cells, giant cells, plasma cells, eosinophils, and neutrophils  - Many histiocytes and giant cells contained intracellular yeasts with a surrounding halo  - Special stains (Grocott-Gomori methenamine-silver nitrate and periodic acid–Schiff) highlighted fungal forms  - Fungal culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar was negative  - HIV-1 and HIV-2 serologic testing were negativeImages:- Figure 1A Title: Tongue ulcer- Figure 1B Title: Biopsy from the ulcer showing a mixed cell infiltrate (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×40)- Figure 1C Title: Intracellular yeast forms within the histiocytes (original magnification ×100)

Case Information: A 64-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with bilateral progressive blurred vision. Medical history includes lung adenocarcinoma managed with partial lobectomy 4 years prior, with local recurrence treated with 6 cycles of carboplatin, pemetrexed, and pembrolizumab. Anterior segment examination unremarkable. Case Information: A woman in her 70s presented with a week of painless, rapidly progressive, edematous, necrotic papules and plaques on the extremities, buttocks, and face with sharp demarcation at the nasolabial folds and extension into the oral mucosa. Notable symptoms included 4 months of extreme fatigue, 20.4 kg weight loss, and a recent episode of hematochezia. Medical history included diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and hypertension that were well controlled with simvastatin, chlorthalidone, hydralazine hydrochloride, lisinopril, and verapamil hydrochloride for 5 years with no new exposures. Age-appropriate cancer screening was up to date.
Physical Examination: Patient was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Examination showed edematous, ulcerated pink plaques confluent on forehead and cheeks with sharp demarcation at nasolabial fold. Retiform purpuric plaque was present on the left leg with overlying desquamation. On hospital day 2, she developed bright red blood per rectum.
Diagnostic Tests: - Laboratory findings: Leukocytosis, normocytic anemia, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, hematuria, and proteinuria. Rheumatological workup showed positive antinuclear antibody titer (1:160), antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody with perinuclear staining (1:1280), myeloperoxidase antibody level of 103 AU/mL, serine proteinase 3 antibody level of 25 AU/mL, and antihistone antibody level of 2.2 U. Negative for double-stranded DNA antibody and antiphospholipid syndrome antibody panel.- Imaging studies: Computed tomography of chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed parenchymal lung nodules.- Pathology:   Image Title: Skin Biopsy Findings  Image Description: Histological examination revealed a neutrophil-rich infiltrate in a predominately perivascular pattern with extravasated erythrocytes, leukocytoclasis with karyorrhectic debris, fibrinoid degeneration of vessels walls, and cryptococcoid forms. Microbial stains (periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott methenamine silver, Gram, and acid-fast bacillus) and tissue cultures were unremarkable.    Lung biopsy showed reactive inflammation and was negative for malignant neoplasm.
Final Diagnosis: Drug-induced ANCA vasculitis secondary to hydralazine

Options.D: Drug-induced ANCA vasculitis secondary to hydralazine

Case Information: An obese man in his mid-30s with no prior systemic or ocular disorders presented to a local emergency department after waking with vision loss in his right eye. The night prior, he had been drinking alcohol heavily and took 2 buprenorphine hydrochloride/naloxone hydrochloride pills. He denied any trauma. He also experienced pain, numbness, and erythematous induration of his right eyelids and forearm that increased throughout the day.
Physical Examination: Visual acuity: No light perception in right eye (OD) and 20/20 in left eye (OS). Right eye showed tense eyelid edema, chemosis, corneal haze, and restricted motility in all fields of gaze. Right pupil was mid-dilated with a relative afferent pupillary defect. Intraocular pressure was 37 mm Hg OD and 21 mm Hg OS. Ophthalmoscopic examination revealed tortuous vessels, serous retinal detachment sparing the inferior periphery, and macular whitening. Left eye examination was normal.
Diagnostic Tests:
- Laboratory Tests:
Creatinine level: 2.2 mg/dL
Creatine kinase level: 29,320 U/L

- Imaging Studies:
1. Noncontrast computed tomography of head and orbits: Showed periorbital soft-tissue swelling

Image Title: OCT of the Right Eye
Image Description: Demonstrates severe disorganization of the retinal architecture, subretinal fluid, and sub-retinal pigment epithelial fluid

3. Fluorescein Angiography:
Image Title: Fluorescein Angiography of the Right Eye
Image Description: Shows delayed choroidal filling, delayed retinal arterial filling, patchy temporal hyperfluorescence, diffuse leakage and poor vascular perfusion in various phases

Case Information: A male patient in the fourth decade of life, born to an Egyptian family and living in France. Case Information: A man in his 50s presented with an abdominal skin eruption of 2 days' duration. His medical history included hepatitis C, cirrhosis, and an orthotopic liver transplant (OLT) 3 years prior that was subsequently treated with tacrolimus, 5 mg, and mycophenolate, 750 mg, twice daily. Five weeks after treatment with CHOP chemotherapy, the patient presented with an acute-onset abdominal skin eruption without fever or pain.

Case Information: A woman in her 80s receiving pembrolizumab treatment (2 mg/kg) for metastatic melanoma of the lung and spine presented with a 2-month history of a worsening vaginal and intergluteal pink-red plaque. She developed the eruption between treatment cycles 2 and 3 of pembrolizumab and was hospitalized. On admission, she was afebrile with mild leukocytosis.
Physical Examination: Physical examination revealed a well-demarcated, thin, pink-red plaque with a red to violaceous rim extending from her mons pubis to her intergluteal folds, with several 3- to 9-mm erosions. She had mild induration of her right perineal skin but no tenderness, fluctuance, or crepitus. There was desquamating yellow scale-crust.
Diagnostic Tests:
- Laboratory tests:
  - Wound cultures: grew 3+ pansensitive Staphylococcus aureus
  - Blood cultures: negative
  - Workup findings were negative for tinea or herpes simplex virus

- Imaging studies:
  - Pelvis CT: normal findings

- Pathological examination:
  - Punch biopsy specimens from right buttocks showed:
    - Psoriasiform hyperplasia with mature keratinocytes
    - Focal spongiosis
    - Superficial, mainly lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate
    - Scattered eosinophils and dermal edema
    - Periodic acid–Schiff staining was negative

- Images:
  Figure 1 Title: Mons Pubis and Bilateral Inguinal Folds
  Description: Smooth pink-red plaque with a red to violaceous rim with multiple 3- to 9-mm erosions and yellow crusting

  Description: Psoriasiform hyperplasia of the epidermis, spongiosis, and a predominantly lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate, with scattered eosinophils and dermal edema (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×10)
Final Diagnosis: Inverse psoriasiform eruption with secondary impetiginization

Options.B: Inverse psoriasiform eruption with secondary impetiginization

Case Information: A 17-month-old boy presented with a slow-growing, nontender plaque on the lower back. The plaque was initially 1 × 1 cm and had grown with the child. Medical history included dermal melanocytosis of the right hip and mid back, increased head circumference (97th percentile), and expressive language delay. No family history of congenital birthmarks.
Physical Examination: Well-appearing boy with normal vital signs and Fitzpatrick type III skin type. On the left lower back, there was a 15 × 5-cm indurated skin-colored to yellow, firm, multinodular plaque with hypertrichosis, extending from the midline to the left lower flank. Additional blue-gray patches were present on the back and right hip, as well as a small café au lait macule on the right lower back. Limited neurologic examination was within normal limits.
Diagnostic Tests: - Biopsy findings:    - Hematoxylin-eosin staining showed diffuse dermal infiltration of spindle cells, predominantly encircling terminal folliculosebaceous units    - Higher-power magnification revealed mix of partially fusiform melanocytes and dendritic cells with glassy, eosinophilic cytoplasm    - Immunohistochemical staining showed diffuse and periadnexal S100 positivity in the mid to deep dermis    - Additional staining: Positive for CD34, SOX-10; Negative for desmin, SMA, CD1a; Partial expression of Melan A and epithelial membrane antigen  - Imaging:    - MRI of lumbar spine showed contrast-enhancing cutaneous lesion extending between L3-L5 spinal segment    - Branches of enhancement extending into paraspinous soft tissues of L4 and deep subcutaneous tissues of L3 spinous process    - No evidence of spinal involvement or dysraphism  Images included:  Figure A: Large, well-defined, firm yellow to skin-colored multinodular hypertrichotic plaque on the left lower back  Figure B: Hematoxylin-eosin staining of dermal infiltration (×4 magnification)  Figure C: Higher-power magnification of melanocytes and dendritic cells (×40 magnification)  Figure D: Immunohistochemical S100 staining (×4 magnification)

Case Information: A woman in her 80s with a history of nonischemic cardiomyopathy and chronic kidney disease presented with purpuric lesions on her face, elbows, knees, and feet. She was initially admitted for altered mental status in the setting of an unwitnessed fall and was noted to have 'bruises' on her lower extremities. New lesions developed on her nose, ear, and the extensor surfaces of her arms bilaterally.
Physical Examination: The patient's nose, bilateral cheeks, forehead, and left ear (helical rim and antihelix) were found to have dusky purpuric macules and patches. Her knees, feet, and the extensor surfaces of her arms had reticulated purpuric macules and patches. There was skin sloughing off the lesions on her elbows and knees.
Diagnostic Tests: - Laboratory tests:     - Hypercalcemia (calcium level, 11.5 mg/dL)    - Acute kidney injury (creatinine level, 5.6 mg/dL)    - Rouleaux and cryoprotein precipitate on peripheral blood smear    - Abnormal paraprotein band on serum and urine protein electrophoreses    - Monoclonal IgG-κ protein on immunofixation electrophoresis    - Elevated serum cryoglobulin levels (cryocrit, 16%)    - Negative results for hepatitis, antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia antibodies, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies  - Biopsy findings:    Four-millimeter punch biopsy specimens from left ear, right arm, and forehead showed multifocal intravascular fibrinoid material consisting of a mix of cryoglobulins and fibrin thrombi with relatively little vessel wall inflammation  - Imaging studies:    CT scan of pelvis revealed lytic bony lesions      - Bone marrow biopsy:    Hypercellular marrow consisting of 80% plasma cells with atypical morphology and κ-light-chain restriction
Final Diagnosis: Type I cryoglobulinemia associated with multiple myeloma

Options.D: Type I cryoglobulinemia associated with multiple myeloma

Case Information: A preschool-age girl presented with an asymptomatic plaque on the right lower extremity that had been present for 1 year. Case Information: A male patient in their early 50s with no history of prior known diseases was admitted with epigastric pain and jaundice of 2 weeks. On the third day of admission, the patient experienced a sudden squeezing pain in the anterior chest at rest, with a heart rate of 44 beats/min, blood pressure of 97/60 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation of 98%. During hospitalization, the patient experienced recurrent episodes of precordial pain 17 times in the following days, with similar pain characteristics as before.
Physical Examination: Initial ECG findings at admission were normal. During chest pain episode: Heart rate 44 beats/min, blood pressure 97/60 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 98%.
Diagnostic Tests: - ECG Studies:    Image A Title: ECG During Chest Pain Attack    Image A Description: Complete atrioventricular block with 4-5mm ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF; 3-6mm ST-segment depression in leads I, aVL, and V1 through V5    Image B Title: ECG After Chest Pain Relief     Image B Description: Normal findings with 53 beats per minute  - Laboratory Tests:    - Troponin I: 0.107 ng/mL (normal: 0-0.034 ng/mL)    - Total bilirubin: 14.08 mg/dL (normal: 0.30-2.92 mg/dL)  - Imaging Studies:    - Echocardiography: Normal cardiac structure and systolic function    - Coronary angiography: Mild nonobstructive disease    - Endoscopic biopsy and PET-CT: Revealed malignant duodenal tumor with peripancreatic metastasis    - Surgical findings: 8 × 6 × 5-cm mass at pancreaticoduodenal junction, upper part invading gallbladder
Final Diagnosis: Cholecystocardial syndrome (CCS) due to poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the pancreaticoduodenal junction

Options.A: Cholecystocardial syndrome (CCS) due to poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the pancreaticoduodenal junction
Options.C: Malignant duodenal tumor with peripancreatic metastasis
Options.D: Malignancy-related autonomic dysfunction with coronary vasospasm

Case Information: A man in his 40s with a 5-year history of mildly pruritic poikilodermatous patches and thin plaques involving the bilateral axilla and groin presented with expanding lesions on both flanks. Physical Examination: There were hypopigmented and hyperpigmented reticulated patches and thin, atrophic plaques covering more than 10% of the total body surface area involving the axilla, groin, and flanks bilaterally. No cervical, axillary, or inguinal lymphadenopathy was noted.

Final Diagnosis: Poikilodermatous mycosis fungoides (PMF) stage IB disease

Options.C: Poikilodermatous mycosis fungoides (PMF) stage IB disease
Options.D: Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma, Not Otherwise Specified

Case Information: A 53-year-old man reported substernal chest pain, lasting less than 5 minutes, which sometimes occurred if he ran more than 2 miles. Case Information: A woman in her 70s with a history of recurrent stasis dermatitis treated with long-term topical and systemic corticosteroids presented to the clinic with painful swelling over the right lower leg of 1 week's duration. Case Information: A school-aged boy presented with occasionally pruritic, generalized hyperkeratotic papules with central white spicules and comedo-like plugs in a linear distribution on his face, trunk, and extremities since birth. Case Information: An elderly man with undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma enrolled in a clinical trial of neoadjuvant treatment with pembrolizumab and radiation therapy. Six months after starting pembrolizumab, he developed gum pain and bleeding.

Case Information: A full-term girl presented at birth with multiple skin lesions. One month later, she returned due to recurring skin eruptions. She was born to healthy, nonconsanguineous parents. Follow-up exam: Multiple round or irregularly shaped erythematous macules and slightly scaly plaques of various sizes on face, trunk, and extremities. Case Information: A man in his 60s with systemic sclerosis presented with a pruritic rash that had been present for 3 months. The patient denied any known preceding triggers or trauma to the area of the rash. He had tried treating with topical aloe, without improvement. Review of systems was negative for any new or worsening constitutional, respiratory, or gastrointestinal symptoms. Past medical history included heart failure, interstitial lung disease, sclerodactyly, and Raynaud phenomenon. He was receiving mycophenolate mofetil, 1 g twice daily. Case Information: A woman in her late 20s presented with an asymptomatic hyperpigmentation on the right side of the trunk, right upper arm, and right leg, strictly following the lines of Blaschko. Case Information: A homosexual man presented with an ulcerative lesion on his penis of 2 months' duration. He had consulted several dermatologists and received different local and systemic treatments including antibiotics, steroids, and antimycotic drugs, with no improvement. The patient had a stable partner and denied both casual and unprotected sex as well as the use of creams or balms on the penis. During counseling, the patient reported using a substance called 'Jungle Juice' during sexual encounters, and could not rule out accidental contact between his contaminated hands and his genitals.
Physical Examination: The shaft of the penis had an asymptomatic, oval ulcer of more than 3 cm on its long axis with undermined borders and a sanious reddish bottom.
Diagnostic Tests:
- Serological Tests: Antibody screening for syphilis and HIV - negative results
- Microbiological Tests: Screening for common bacteria and yeasts - negative results
- PCR Testing: Tests for Treponema and Chlamydia species - negative results
- Histologic Analysis: Full epidermal necrosis with infiltration of neutrophils and eosinophils. A diffuse dermal inflammatory infiltrate rich in polymorphonucleocytes, and focal fibrinoid necrosis of superficial vessels
- Patch Testing: International Contact Dermatitis Research Group standard series and single patch test with alkyl nitrite preparation at 2% in water - negative at 48 and 72 hours

Case Information: A woman in her late 50s was hospitalized in March 2020 for severe bilateral pneumonia. She had recent close contact with a fatal case. No relevant medical history was reported. On day 2 post-admission, she developed blurred vision and redness in her right eye and temporary (8-day) pain when mobilizing the globe.
Physical Examination: Best-corrected visual acuity was +2 logMAR (hand movement) OD and 0 logMAR OS. The right eye had:- Relative afferent pupil defect- Central scotoma- Impaired color and contrast vision- Central nongranulomatous retrodescemetic precipitates - Mild anterior chamber inflammation- Noticeable pupillary edema- 2 peripapillary hemorrhages- Mild vitreous inflammation- Retinal vessel narrowing in the inferior retinaContralateral eye examinations were normal. No other neurological symptoms were observed.
Diagnostic Tests: - Laboratory Tests:  * Normal complete blood cell counts  * Normal serum angiotensin-converting enzyme levels  * Normal human leukocyte antigen B51/B27 typing  * Negative results for syphilis, HIV, Toxoplasma gondii, and Borrelia serologies  * Negative IgM and very weakly positive IgG for VZV, HSV, EBV, and CMV  * Positive nasopharyngeal swab RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2  * Negative CSF SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR- Imaging Studies:  * Cranial MRI with fine optic nerve cuts (normal results)  * Fluorescein Angiography (Day 30):    Image Title: Optic disc neuritis    Image Description: Mild leakage associated with inferior peripapillary hemorrhage        Image Title: Retinal vasculitis    Image Description: Fluorescein leakage from retinal venules inferotemporal to the macula    * Papillary OCT (Days 30 & 48):    Image Description: Progression from discrete right papillary edema to severe optic nerve atrophy
Final Diagnosis: Inflammation-induced ocular neuropathy associated with SARS-CoV-2–induced panuveitis

Options.C: COVID-19-associated optic neuritis and retinal vasculitis
Options.D: Inflammation-induced ocular neuropathy associated with SARS-CoV-2–induced panuveitis

Case Information: A woman in her 50s presented with a 3-month history of rapidly spreading intensively pruritic papules on her extremities. Case Information: A patient in their 80s presented with dyspnea and syncope during exercise. Medical history included essential hypertension and Parkinson disease. Case Information: A man in his 20s presented with a 6-year history of multiple growing papules superimposed on an asymptomatic firm plaque on the occipital scalp. The lesions were never ulcerated or inflamed, but hemorrhage occurred occasionally after rubbing. At 3 years of age, scarlike macules appeared on the occipital scalp and coalesced to form a larger plaque with sparse hair. Simultaneously, multiple brown-red, dome-shaped papules developed on the nose and gradually evolved to involve the cheeks. Rubbery plaques also developed on the sacrococcygeal area, along with hypopigmented patches on the right buttock. The patient has no systemic symptoms or mental impairment and denied a family history of genetic disease.

Case Information: A 13-month-old girl was referred for evaluation of an asymptomatic, solid nasopharyngeal mass found incidentally on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) obtained for evaluation of a morning glory disc anomaly at age 11 months. The patient was asymptomatic and had normal hormone levels including insulin-like growth factor 1, thyroid-stimulating hormone, free thyroxine, and adrenocorticotropic hormone.
Physical Examination: Flexible fiberoptic nasopharyngoscopy through the nares revealed a smooth, pedunculated lesion predominantly obstructing the right choana and adherent to the posterior pharyngeal wall by a stalk. Additional tissue was evident inferiorly within the craniopharyngeal canal. Case Information: A woman in her late 30s presented with a 4-day history of perianal pain. Her medical history included systemic lupus erythematosus, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, and external hemorrhoids. Six months prior, she underwent a deceased donor kidney transplant. Current medications included prednisone 5 mg daily and mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg twice daily. She developed diarrhea 1 day after admission.
Physical Examination: On admission, she was afebrile and normotensive. Total body skin examination revealed 1- and 3-cm tender, round perianal ulcers with a clean base. Another 4-mm round ulcer was present at the superior intergluteal cleft. There were no ocular or oral ulcers.

Case Information: A man in his 50s presented with an asymptomatic, arc-shaped, depressed skin groove on the left side of his forehead, frontal scalp, and vertex area. Localized linear hair loss and hair thinning on the left scalp area were observed. The patient reported that when the lesion had begun approximately 10 years earlier, he had received 2 doses of intralesional steroid via injection on a small bald patch on the vertex. Thereafter, the lesion gradually progressed to the frontal scalp and eventually made a linear furrow on the left side of his forehead. The patient denied any trauma history and had no history of connective tissue disease nor any evidence of systemic involvement, such as arthralgia, photosensitivity, or skin rashes.
Physical Examination: Examination revealed 2 long, curved-line, depressed, alopecic patches on the left side of the vertex and frontal scalp area extending to the left eyebrow. The lesions measured (length × width) 7 × 2 cm and 6 × 1 cm, respectively. Case Information: A neonate in her second week of life with a scalp lesion. Born full term to a primigravid mother with uncomplicated pregnancy. Case Information: A previously healthy 16-year-old girl presented with a red tumor on her right upper arm that enlarged over 6 months. Case Information: A woman in her 50s presented to the emergency department after a fall. She reported being clumsy her entire life, with worsening difficulty with balance over the past few years. She occasionally had falls, which were sometimes preceded by vertigo and 'shaking' episodes.

Case Information: A 42-year-old man with sinonasal polyposis and nasal septal deviation, with no previous sinus surgery. Prior to surgery, visual acuity was 20/20 OU without correction.

Case Information: A male patient in his 20s presented with a 12-month history of asymptomatic red to brown macules and papules that initially appeared on his trunk and subsequently spread to the upper and proximal lower extremities. The lesions were symmetrically distributed and did not coalesce. His face, distal extremities, and mucous membranes were unaffected. The patient reported that some lesions had resolved spontaneously with residual hyperpigmentation. His medical history was unremarkable, and he did not take any medication on a regular basis.
Physical Examination: - Multiple red to brown macules and papules on trunk and extremities- Symmetrically distributed lesions that did not coalesce- Face, distal extremities, and mucous membranes unaffected- No lymphadenopathy- Other systems review unremarkable
Diagnostic Tests: Laboratory Tests:- Blood cell count showed hypereosinophilia (4220/μL; reference range 50-250/μL)- Elevated tryptase (33.7 ng/mL; reference range <11.5 ng/mL)- Elevated vitamin B12 (>6000 pg/mL; reference range 211-911 pg/mL)- Negative serologic tests for HIV, hepatitis A, B, and C- Negative tests for parasitic infectionsImaging Studies:- CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis: no pathologic findings- Cranial MRI: no pathologic findingsPathological Findings:- Skin biopsy (chest and upper extremity):  - Nodular infiltration of histiocytes with lymphocytes and eosinophils in upper dermis  - No lipid-laden foam cells or multinucleated giant cells  - Immunohistochemistry: CD68 positive, stabilin 1 positive, S-100 protein weakly positive, CD1a negativeBone Marrow Analysis:- Hypercellularity with myeloid hyperplasia- Increased eosinophils (20%, reference range <5%)- FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion gene positive on RT-PCR
Final Diagnosis: FIP1L1-PDGFRA–positive chronic eosinophilic leukemia (CEL) with associated generalized eruptive histiocytosis (GEH)

Options.A: Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia and FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion
Options.C: FIP1L1-PDGFRA–positive chronic eosinophilic leukemia (CEL) with associated generalized eruptive histiocytosis (GEH)

Case Information: A woman in her 50s with a history of recent hospitalization for congestive heart failure developed a painful ulceration on the right distal forearm at a previous peripheral intravenous catheter site. Case Information: A man in his 70s presented as a transfer for evaluation of a hypopharyngeal mass. The day prior, the patient had an episode of nausea and violent vomiting, after which a bilobed, cylindrical mucosal mass was expelled from his mouth. Case Information: A patient in their 20s presented to the emergency department complaining of severe midsternal chest pain of several hours' duration. The patient was in very good health before their presentation. The patient was not taking any medications and had no risk factors for coronary artery disease. They used cocaine 3 to 4 hours before presentation.
Physical Examination: Patient was thin, anxious, and in acute distress. The patient was diaphoretic and tachypneic. Blood pressure was 138/80 mm Hg with a regular pulse of 180 beats per minute; no fever. The patient had a questionable S4, but otherwise their examination was unremarkable.
Diagnostic Tests: - Laboratory tests: Initial laboratory results were unremarkable except for elevated creatine phosphokinase level and myocardial band consistent with myocardial injury.- Imaging studies:  1. ECG (Initial):     Title: Regular wide QRS tachycardia     Description: Alternating QRS morphology and frontal-plane QRS axis. QRS complexes have variable right bundle branch block–like morphology in V1. Anterior ST segment depression noted.    2. ECG (Repeated):     Title: Ectopic atrial/junctional rhythm     Description: Severe ST segment depression in the midprecordial leads. Inverted P waves in inferior leads. Normal frontal-plane QRS axis.    3. Heart Catheterization:     Description: Mild haziness in the mid left anterior descending artery without significant stenosis    4. Echocardiogram:     Description: Severe hypokinesis of the anterior wall, mid and distal anterior septum, and apex. Left ventricular ejection fraction estimated at around 30%
Final Diagnosis: Bidirectional ventricular tachycardia (BVT) induced by cocaine use with associated myocardial injury

Options.A: Bidirectional ventricular tachycardia (BVT) induced by cocaine use with associated myocardial injury
Options.C: Cocaine-induced acute myocardial infarction (due to coronary vasospasm)

Case Information: A woman in her 40s presented with blurred vision in the right eye. She was undergoing treatment with systemic steroids, durvalumab (a PD-L1 inhibitor), and bevacizumab. Ten days after initial presentation, the patient developed sudden vision loss in the right eye.
Physical Examination: Initial examination: Visual acuity of 20/25 OU. Right eye showed full visual field, right-sided relative afferent pupillary defect, unremarkable anterior segment, and mild swelling of the optic disc. Left eye had normal fundus and visual function. Follow-up examination (after vision loss): Right eye showed no light perception vision, marked swelling of the optic disc, peripapillary retinal hemorrhages, and occlusion of the superior branch artery. Two days later: Combined occlusion of the central retinal artery and vein, and a new collection of whitish material suspended anterior to the optic disc, forming a pocket in the posterior vitreous.
Diagnostic Tests: - Imaging Studies:    Image Title: MRI at Onset of Vision Loss    Image Description:     - Coronal T1-weighted contrast-enhanced image: Focal enhancement along enlarged right optic nerve    - Axial T1-weighted contrast-enhanced image: Diffuse enlargement of orbital portion of right optic nerve, enhancement of nerve sheath, slight flattening of posterior globe    - Coronal T2-weighted (FLAIR) image: Hyperintensity of right optic nerve  - Laboratory Tests:    - Lumbar puncture showed no abnormalities      - Other Tests:    - Wide-field fluorescein angiography: Showed choroidal flush but complete lack of perfusion of retinal vasculature      - Pathological Examination:    - Vitreous biopsy: Hypercellular sample with astrocytic neoplasm, small to medium-sized cells with scant cytoplasm and oval, pleomorphic, hyperchromatic nuclei    - Immunohistochemistry: Positive for glial fibrillary acid protein, oligodendrocyte transcription factor 2, mutant IDH-1 protein, p53; Loss of ATRX protein; Ki-67 proliferation index ~10%
Final Diagnosis: Glioblastoma (World Health Organization grade IV) with optic nerve invasion and intraocular extension

Case Information: An adolescent girl with history of polycystic ovarian syndrome presented with hyperpigmented skin lesions affecting her neck, upper limbs, and trunk. The lesions had started about 6 months previously as recurrent crops of pruritic erythematous papules that subsided leaving behind brownish-bluish black hyperpigmentation after each episode. No history suggestive of allergic rhinitis or bronchial asthma. Her fasting blood glucose and basal insulin levels were not raised. No family history of similar lesions.
Physical Examination: Multiple brown hyperpigmented patches symmetrically affecting neck, axillae, antecubital fossa, and intermammary and inframammary areas. Patches showed reticulate pattern at peripheries. Intermammary patches had central erythema and few subsiding papules. Dark brown to bluish-gray patches with reticulation present on lower back and dorsum of neck, with few resolving erythematous papules in periphery. Rest of skin, nails, and mucosae were normal.

Case Information: A Chinese woman in her late 20s presented with a 20-year history of progressive skin laxity. The patient had no extracutaneous involvement and was born to healthy nonconsanguineous parents. Her younger sister had developed the same skin symptoms.

Asn389Lys fs*13) in exon 8     - c.824C>T (p. Ser275Leu) in exon 7
Final Diagnosis: Pseudoxanthoma elasticum-like disorder with coagulation deficiency

Case Information: A 52-year-old Japanese woman presented with a 2-year history of swelling of her right upper eyelid, which had discharged pus for the previous 10 months without any trauma to her head. Case Information: An African American woman in her 30s with no medical history presented with a 4-year history of diffuse progressive proliferation of dark papules. The lesions initially began on her thighs and rapidly multiplied throughout her skin. Some lesions were pruritic and when scratched could be removed, leaving behind a hyperpigmented macule. The patient described a sunburn several weeks prior to the initial eruption. She was taking no medications and these lesions were unchanged throughout an uncomplicated pregnancy. No personal or family history of melanoma or eruptive nevi.
Physical Examination: Hundreds of 1- to 2-mm dark brown-black monomorphic papules throughout trunk, extremities, palms, face, tongue, and sclera. No lymphadenopathy present.
Diagnostic Tests: - Laboratory tests: Complete blood cell count and comprehensive metabolic panel were unremarkable.- Imaging studies: Computed tomography of chest was unremarkable.- Pathology:  Image Title: Punch biopsy of right arm (Figure B-C)  Image Description: Shows circumscribed proliferation of pigmented epithelioid melanocytic nests, located primarily at tips of rete ridges. Moderate cytologic atypia present. Superficial papillary dermis shows prominent pigment incontinence. No mitotic figures seen. Kamino bodies not visualized.    Image Title: Melan-A immunostain (Figure D)  Image Description: Shows low pagetoid migration of melanocytes with a lack of melanocytic confluence at the dermal-epidermal junction.

Case Information: A man in his 40s presented with sudden-onset slurring of speech and imbalance on walking. He had difficulty swallowing and required a nasogastric tube for feeding. Six months previously, he had left-sided hemiparesis, which had improved significantly. On day 5 of admission, purposeless tapping movements were observed in the patient's right hand. The movements were repetitive, of the same type, and lasted for 30 seconds to 5 minutes. The patient was able to suppress these movements at will. These movements were not preceded by an urge to perform them, and on stopping, there was no development of internal tension. The movements were not associated with any change in sensorium or incontinence. The movements slowly decreased in severity but maintained the same pattern. He was discharged on day 28 when the movements were very mild. At the 1-month follow-up, the movements had almost disappeared.
Physical Examination: The patient demonstrated repetitive tapping movements in the right hand that could be voluntarily suppressed.
Diagnostic Tests: - Imaging Studies:    Image Title: Magnetic Resonance Imaging of the Brain    Image Description: T1, T2, diffusion-weighted, and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) axial images showing:    - Acute infarct in left thalamic region (isointense on T1, hyperintense on T2, hyperintense on diffusion, hypointense on ADC)    - Old infarct in right gangliocapsular region        - Other Tests:    Electroencephalogram (day 7): No abnormalities        - Video Documentation:    Title: Right Hand Stereotypy    Description: Stereotypic movements of the right hand in the form of repeated tapping; patient able to stop the tapping when asked to do so
Final Diagnosis: Post-stroke stereotypy secondary to acute left thalamic infarct

Options.B: Post-stroke stereotypy secondary to acute left thalamic infarct

Case Information: A healthy woman in her 60s presented with multiple erythematous crusted plaques on her trunk that had appeared 4 weeks previously, sparing her limbs and facial region. She had a long-standing history of several outbreaks of skin lesions limited to both axillae and groin. Previous episodes had been successfully treated with various topical drugs administered by her primary care physician. No family history of similar lesions was recorded.
Physical Examination: Multiple annular erythematous plaques surrounded by a peripheral crusted and pustular collarette on her trunk. No active lesions were present in her axillae, inframammary folds, or groin.
Diagnostic Tests: - Histopathologic examination (H&E stain):  Image Title: Histopathologic images, hematoxylin-eosin  Image Description: Revealed wide areas of suprabasilar acantholysis showing a 'dilapidated brick wall' morphologic characteristic. The epidermis was focally covered by a neutrophil-rich serous crust located in the overlying stratum corneum. A mild inflammatory infiltrate was identified on superficial papillary dermis.- Direct immunofluorescence:  Results: Negative for IgG, IgA, IgM, fibrin, and complement deposition- Microbiological culture:  Results: Staphylococcus aureus isolated from pustular exudate- Clinical Images:  Image Title: Multiple erythematous and crusted plaques  Image Description: Diffusely distributed on the dorsal trunk at presentation    Image Title: Erythematous annular plaque  Image Description: Surrounded by a crusted and focally pustular peripheral collarette

Case Information: A man in his early 50s with a history of human immunodeficiency virus, type 1 diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia presented for a routine diabetic screening examination without ophthalmic complaints. He had a history of infection 10 years prior to presentation, which was treated with oral penicillin. His rapid plasma reagin was nonreactive 1 year prior to presentation.
Physical Examination: Visual acuity was 20/20 − 3 OD and 20/20 − 1 OS. Anterior segment and vitreous were unremarkable without inflammation in both eyes. Dilated ophthalmoscopy revealed a neurosensory detachment in the inferior macula of the right eye including the fovea. Subretinal yellow lesions smaller than 100 μm in diameter were present, as was slightly elevated, poorly demarcated yellow discoloration in the central portion of the neurosensory detachment. The left fundus was within normal limits.

No late leakage from peripheral vasculature or optic nerve.        2. Optical coherence tomography:       Image Title: Optical Coherence Tomography Through the Center of the Neurosensory Detachment       Image Description: Demonstrated shallow subretinal fluid with hyperreflective foci predominantly within the outer retina. Case Information: A man in his 60s presented to the emergency department with 5 days of nausea and vomiting. He noted chronic, left-sided abdominal pain and normal passage of stool and flatus. Past medical history was unremarkable. Current medications included only esomeprazole.
Physical Examination: Vital signs: Afebrile, normotensive, pulse rate 104/minute. Abdominal exam revealed a large, firm, tender mass located near the umbilicus, without rigidity or rebound tenderness.
Diagnostic Tests: - Laboratory studies:    - Lactate: 6.3 mmol/L (reference range 0.7-2.2 mmol/L)    - Serial lactate measurements between 4.7-7.2 mmol/L    - Low bicarbonate, low PCO2, marginally acidotic pH on venous blood gas    - Urinalysis and blood cultures showed no evidence of infection      - Imaging studies:    CT Abdomen findings: Diffuse lymphadenopathy and a large mesenteric mass abutting multiple segments of small intestine and encasing the mesenteric vasculature
Final Diagnosis: Type B lactic acidosis secondary to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

Options.A: Small bowel ischemia due to mesenteric lymphoma
Options.C: Type B lactic acidosis secondary to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
